subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: dividing tasks by strengths and delegating [Action]
passage:
Week 1. Lakshmi and Pema wrote three lists. Lakshmi took decor and outfits, Pema took travel and vendors, and the cousins agreed to sort out the guest rooms.

Week 4. On the Sunday call, everyone reported in two minutes each. Pema had booked the bus. A cousin had found a guest house with twelve rooms and sent a photo. Lakshmi's tailor promised the outfits by the twentieth.

Week 9. In wedding week the tempo carrying the decor broke down. Pema rang the backup transporter from the vendor list, and it took ten minutes. Nobody panicked. The Sunday call had made everyone used to speaking up early.

qa.q: Who took charge of decor and outfits?
How did Lakshmi probably feel when the decor tempo broke down?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt a flash of worry, but stayed calm because the backup was already on the vendor list.

qa.q: What else could the group do to keep things smooth, and why?
qa.a: They could keep a shared list of who to call for each problem, because a quick contact list saves time when something breaks.

qa.q: How might a cousin in charge of guest rooms have found the weekly call?
qa.a: A cousin would probably find it helpful and encouraging, since the two-minute reports showed the work was seen and everyone was informed.

grounding: Illustrates dividing wedding tasks by strengths, with the bride on decor and outfits, the groom on travel and vendors and cousins on rooms, with a weekly call.

subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: dividing tasks by strengths and delegating [Action]
passage:
Jyoti, you're drowning in wedding lists? Sit. Let me, Gurleen, tell you how your Masi and Mausa managed ours in Ludhiana, back in 2001.
I was good with colours, so I took decor and outfits. Your Mausa, Harjit, could talk to anyone and never lost a receipt, so he took travel and all the vendors: tent, caterer, band. My cousins Pinky and Bittu took the guest rooms, who stays where, who needs a mattress on the floor.
Every Sunday at eight, we all gathered on the landline. Each person said three things: done, stuck, need help. Ten minutes, no more.
Two days before the wedding, the tent man said he was short of chairs. Harjit already knew, from Sunday's call, and had a second supplier ready.
My friends' weddings that year were chaos at the last minute. Ours wasn't perfect, Jyoti, but nobody was running around crying.

qa.q: What time was the Sunday call?
How did Gurleen feel about the wedding compared with friends' weddings that year?
qa.a: Gurleen felt proud and relieved that their wedding wasn't chaotic at the last minute, even if it wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Gurleen's story, and why did the weekly call matter there?
qa.a: The turning point was the chair shortage two days before; because of Sunday's call, Harjit already knew and had a second supplier ready.

qa.q: How might Pinky and Bittu have felt with the guest rooms as their job?
qa.a: They probably felt useful and trusted, with a clear job of their own instead of vague chores.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how the bride took decor and outfits, the groom travel and vendors, cousins the guest rooms, and a weekly call reduced last-minute chaos.

subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: dividing tasks by strengths and delegating [Action]
passage:
With his leave approved for only ten days and the wedding in Thrissur, Ujjwal had to plan most of it from his desk in Bengaluru.
Nirmala, his fiancée, took decor and outfits; she had been sketching the stage for months. Ujjwal took travel and vendors, since he could make calls on lunch breaks. His cousin Jeevan and two other cousins in Thrissur took charge of guest rooms at the family house and two nearby lodges.
Every Wednesday at nine at night, the five of them joined a video call. Each person said what was done and what was stuck. Twenty minutes, then goodnight.
Three weeks before the wedding, the lodge Jeevan had booked cancelled. Jeevan raised it on Wednesday's call, and by Friday Ujjwal had found another near the temple.
On the wedding morning, Nirmala's sister was amazed. "Nobody is shouting," she said. Ujjwal just grinned, tired but calm.

qa.q: What time was the weekly video call?
qa.a: Every Wednesday at nine at night.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel on the wedding morning?
qa.a: He felt tired but calm and happy, grinning because the plan had held together.

qa.q: What else could the group add to handle a surprise closer to the date?
qa.a: They could agree on a quick message rule for urgent problems between calls, so a cancellation in the last week doesn't wait for Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt when the lodge cancelled?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt worried and responsible, but raising it on the call meant help came quickly instead of carrying the problem alone.

grounding: It shows the bride handling decor and outfits, the groom travel and vendors, cousins the guest rooms, and a weekly call keeping everyone informed despite limited leave.
